summary: Describes the media transport aspects of WebRTC, specifying how the Real-time Transport Protocol is used and which RTP features, profiles and extensions are required of implementations.

eli5.summary: How audio and video get packed and sent in a browser call, and which features every browser must support.

questions: what rtp features does webrtc require
what rtp profile does webrtc require
subtitle: Which parts of RTP every WebRTC endpoint must implement to send audio and video between browsers.

tldr.problem: The Real-time Transport Protocol has accumulated many profiles, payload formats and extensions, so new WebRTC implementations need to know which ones to support to interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8834 sets a baseline: RTP with RTCP over the secure RTP/SAVPF profile, multiplexed on one flow, plus mandated feedback messages and header extensions, loss-repair tools, and congestion-control rules.
tldr.outcome: WebRTC endpoints share a common RTP feature set. The RFC notes there is no standard congestion control algorithm for interactive media yet, so endpoints must use their own plus the RTP circuit breaker.

facts.label: Unencrypted SRTP bytes
facts.value: first 12 bytes of the RTP header

today: RFC 8834 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2021 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It says that if a standard congestion control algorithm for interactive media is developed, the memo will need to be updated to mandate it.

sections.title: Why a WebRTC RTP Baseline
sections.content:
The Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) is a framework for delivering audio, video and other real-time media, with many profiles, payload formats and extensions defined over the years. WebRTC provides building blocks for direct, interactive communication between two peers' web browsers. This memo describes how RTP is to be used in that context.

The RFC builds on the past 20 years of RTP development. It mandates extensions that have shown widespread utility while staying compatible with the wide installed base of RTP implementations where possible. RTP and RTCP extensions it does not discuss may still be implemented if they help new use cases, but they are not needed for the WebRTC requirements in RFC 7478.

The memo specifies a protocol intended for WebRTC but not restricted to it. The RFC expects the baseline to be broadly useful for other conferencing uses, such as desktop or mobile video-conferencing systems and room-based telepresence.
sections.eli5: RTP has lots of optional add-ons. This document picks the ones every browser must have, so a call between any two browsers works.

sections.title: Core Protocols Every Endpoint Needs
sections.content:
RTP is REQUIRED as the media transport protocol for WebRTC, and its control part, RTCP, MUST be implemented and used. Features that limited implementations sometimes omit are required here, including multiple simultaneous synchronization sources (SSRCs) in one session, random SSRC choice with collision detection, reception of contributing source (CSRC) lists from mixers, correct sender report timing for lip sync, and support for Sender Report, Receiver Report, Source Description and BYE packets. Endpoints must also ignore unknown RTCP packet types and RTP header extensions.

For the profile, the extended secure RTP profile for RTCP-based feedback (RTP/SAVPF) MUST be implemented. Endpoints MUST NOT send packets using the basic RTP/AVP or RTP/AVPF profiles, so SRTP and SRTCP are always used, configured as described in RFC 8827.

Several choices are made to ease NAT and firewall traversal and reduce ports:

  • Endpoints are REQUIRED to support all media types in a single RTP session on one transport-layer flow (SSRC multiplexing), and also separate sessions per media type for legacy interworking.
  • RTP and RTCP multiplexing on one flow is REQUIRED and must be negotiated in signaling.
  • Sending and receiving non-compound (reduced size) RTCP feedback packets MUST be supported, and negotiated, with compound RTCP as the fallback.
  • Symmetric RTP is REQUIRED, so flows are bidirectional, which helps keep NAT and firewall pinholes alive.

Each RTP payload type number MUST NOT be assigned to different payload formats or configurations within one session. Each endpoint MUST have at least one RTCP CNAME and MUST NOT use more than one CNAME within a single RTCPeerConnection. The CNAME MUST be a new, short-term persistent value following RFC 7022, to avoid tracking users.
sections.eli5: Every browser must use the locked, secure version of the delivery service, put everything through one door to keep the network happy, and give each sender a fresh name tag for each call.

sections.title: Conferencing Feedback and Header Extensions
sections.content:
The conferencing extensions are meant for centralized setups where an RTP middlebox such as a conference bridge distributes streams. Endpoints that skip them still work but may perform poorly. The RFC says endpoints are not expected to support IP multicast or single-session mesh topologies, but a mesh made of several RTP sessions (independent RTCPeerConnections) is expected. Video-switching MCUs and the Relay-Transport Translator topology SHOULD NOT be used, and content-modifying MCUs with RTCP termination MAY be used.

Senders MUST understand and react to Full Intra Request (FIR), Picture Loss Indication (PLI) and Temporary Maximum Media Stream Bit Rate Request (TMMBR) messages, and MUST follow bandwidth limits set by a TMMBR for their SSRC. Receivers are RECOMMENDED to send Slice Loss Indication when slices are lost, and SHOULD send Reference Picture Selection Indication when the codec supports it.

RTP header extensions are OPTIONAL, but when used they MUST follow RFC 8285 and only carry data that can safely be ignored. Some are mandated: the client-to-mixer audio level extension MUST be implemented, the media stream identification (MID) extension MUST be implemented by endpoints using SDP bundle, and the video orientation extension MUST be implemented by endpoints that send or receive video. Rapid synchronization is RECOMMENDED. Audio level extensions must be encryptable, because the information can be sensitive.
sections.eli5: When many people join a video meeting through a central server, the server can ask a sender for a fresh full picture or to slow down. Senders must listen and obey.

sections.title: Coping With Packet Loss
sections.content:
Loss-repair tools add overhead, so the combined bitrate MUST still be rate controlled to avoid congestion. Because of RTP/SAVPF, endpoints can send negative acknowledgements (NACKs). Senders are REQUIRED to understand the generic NACK but may ignore some or all of it. Receivers MAY send NACKs and are not expected to send one for every lost packet.

Retransmission using the RTP retransmission payload format (RFC 4588) needs care in interactive applications. It can work well when the network round-trip time is low, but it can raise bandwidth use and worsen loss caused by congestion. Receivers are REQUIRED to support retransmission packets sent using SSRC multiplexing, and senders need not retransmit every NACKed packet.

Forward Error Correction (FEC) protects against some loss at the cost of steady bandwidth overhead and increased play-out delay. Endpoints MUST follow the FEC recommendations in RFC 8854, and any other FEC type MUST be negotiated before use.
sections.eli5: If a packet of the video goes missing, the receiver can ask for it again or the sender can include spare pieces. But a late repair is useless in a live call, so both sides have to be choosy.

sections.title: Rate Control and Monitoring
sections.content:
WebRTC runs over networks with very different delays and capacities, so endpoints MUST ensure the RTP traffic they generate adapts to match changes in available capacity. The RFC states that at the time of writing there is no standard congestion control algorithm for interactive media like WebRTC flows. Requirements for such algorithms are in RFC 8836, and the congestion control used will have to be proprietary until a standard exists.

Endpoints MUST implement the RTP circuit breaker of RFC 8083, which reacts to extreme congestion. Because it might not trigger until congestion is extreme, it is not a substitute for congestion control, which MUST also be implemented. Bandwidth limits received in signaling, such as SDP b=AS: or b=CT: lines, MUST be followed, and a receiver SHOULD signal its own limits. Anything that interworks with WebRTC MUST implement RTCP and provide congestion feedback through it.

For monitoring, Sender Reports and Receiver Reports, which carry packet-loss and jitter statistics, are REQUIRED. RTCP Extended Reports (XR) are not required, and unexpected or unknown XR packets MUST be ignored.
sections.eli5: The internet is shared like a road. Each browser must slow down when the road is jammed, and there is an emergency brake for when things get really bad.

sections.title: Signaling, API and Implementation Notes
sections.content:
RTP assumes an external signaling channel configures the session. The parameters that must be agreed are the RTP profile (RTP/SAVPF, which MUST be signaled), transport information (supplied by ICE in WebRTC), payload types and format parameters, RTP extensions, and RTCP bandwidth. They are often carried in SDP offer/answer messages, but RTP does not depend on SDP.

In the WebRTC API, a MediaStreamTrack is realized as a source packet stream identified by an SSRC, and it may add dependent or redundancy streams with their own SSRCs. Each track added to an RTCPeerConnection SHALL give an independent source packet stream. A WebRTC endpoint MUST support receiving multiple tracks that use different CNAMEs, though tracks with different CNAMEs have no defined synchronization.

The implementation section describes why an endpoint might use several media sources in one session (multiple media types, multiple capture devices, repair data, layered coding, mixers) or several RTP sessions (legacy devices, quality-of-service separation, separate purposes, a multi-unicast mesh, or mixers). It also notes that SRTP leaves the first 12 bytes of the RTP header unencrypted, so deep packet inspectors can still classify streams. It covers SSRC collision scenarios, including an RTP middlebox that loops an endpoint's traffic back to it, and says that media synchronization relies on a shared CNAME and on RTCP Sender Reports in NTP format.
sections.eli5: The browsers need a separate way to agree on the settings before the call, such as a phone call to arrange the video call. The rest of this part is advice on how to build the plumbing.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC believes there are no new security considerations from combining these protocols; the considerations of RTP, RTP/SAVPF and the extensions all apply, along with the WebRTC security architecture of RFC 8827. RTP/SAVPF plus DTLS-SRTP keying (RFC 5764) gives the mandatory-to-implement media security, offering confidentiality, integrity and partial source authentication.

Long-term persistent CNAMEs can be used to track users across calls, which is why short-term persistent CNAMEs are mandated. A misconfigured RTCP reporting interval can enable denial of service: too large an interval can prevent effective congestion control, too small a one can cause uncontrolled RTCP traffic, and mismatched settings can cause premature participant timeouts. Endpoints SHOULD ignore parameters that set the interval significantly longer than the default five-second interval from RFC 3550 (unless the media rate is so low that it roughly matches 5% of the media data rate), or small enough that RTCP bandwidth would exceed media bandwidth.

RTP middleboxes are trusted nodes: they must maintain confidentiality and integrity and perform source authentication, and they can prevent one endpoint from impersonating another. Encrypting audio-level header extensions is RECOMMENDED.

This document has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Mostly the existing locks are enough. Take care not to use a name tag that follows you from call to call, and do not let anyone set the check-in timer to something silly.
